title: Gathering sparks
hookLine: each good act lifts a spark back to its source

lines: SOMEONE HAS TO PICK IT UP.
cards: In the book of Ruth, a widow walks into a barley field after the reapers have gone through. She isn't harvesting. She's gleaning: bending down, again and again, for the stalks that fell and were left behind.
Slow work, done close to the ground, one stalk at a time. By evening she has enough to carry home to Naomi. Luria's followers gave every person a job that looks a lot like hers.
The light fell. Now someone has to bend down and pick it up.

teach.b: Gathering sparks. In Hebrew, the lifting of the sparks. First, where the sparks are.

After the breaking, Luria's teaching says, sparks of holy light lie scattered, wrapped in husks. The Hebrew word is kelipot: shells or peels that hide the light the way a peel hides the fruit. Second, who gathers.
In this picture, people do. A commandment kept, an act of kindness, a blessing said with care: each one frees a spark from its husk and lifts it back toward its source.
For Luria's followers, the commandments weren't only rules. They were a way of gathering. Third, the ordinary places.
Hasidic teachers carried this out into daily life and found sparks everywhere: in the food on a plate, in the tools of a trade, on the road to work.
Eat with a blessing, deal honestly, speak kindly, and the thing in your hand is lifted.

Some Hasidic stories say a person is led to a certain town, a certain meal, a certain stranger, because a spark there was waiting for them in particular. Fourth, the size of the job. Nobody gathers all of it.
Each person has their own sparks, the teaching goes, and the work happens one at a time, like Ruth bending in the field.
A shard, picked up and set right. That's why today's line is so small. Not the whole world yet.

how: In Hasidic communities, the idea of lifting sparks is taught as a reason to say blessings over food and to treat work, travel and ordinary objects with care, since each can hold something holy.

o: collecting the ashes of a fire for a ritual offering
freeing holy sparks through good acts, one at a time
picking up grain the reapers leave at harvest

s: in this teaching, sparks are found only in holy places
Hasidic teachers found them in food, in a trade, on the road to work.
the husks are pictured like peels that hide the light
kelipot: shells around the fruit, hiding what's inside.
one person is meant to gather all the sparks
each person has their own; the work happens one at a time.

games.q: you sit down to an ordinary meal. in Hasidic teaching on the sparks, what can this moment be?
o: nothing much: holiness happens somewhere else.
a chance to lift a spark, by eating with a blessing.
games.why: Hasidic teachers saw sparks in food itself: a blessing and a careful meal lift the spark hidden in it.

practice: Look through your day for one small thing that's out of place: a loose button, a drawer that sticks, a message you never answered, a word said too sharply.
Choose just one, and picture yourself setting it right, slowly and with care, as if something hidden in it were being lifted. Notice how small it is, and let that be enough.

wordCard.voice: Gathering sparks. In Luria's teaching and in Hasidic life, each good act frees a spark from its husk and lifts it back toward its source. Today's words.

carryVoice: Your line: repair a shard. Nobody gathers all of it, and nobody has to. Until tomorrow.
